editorial.linkPolicy: Append at most one own-site URL from linkPath. Paths are canonical editorial targets without platform suffixes. The publisher chooses the platform suffix.
editorial.sequencePolicy: Sort by sequence for an alternating career, education, nomad/community reading order. Sequence is not a publication date or an API scheduling instruction.
editorial.examplesPolicy: Worked examples and sample wording are teaching exercises, not client results, testimonials, market statistics or reported anecdotes.
editorial.visualPolicy: Each visual is a production brief. Use educational diagrams or genuine product screenshots. Keep screenshots focused on evergreen controls and field labels. No invented interfaces, live job listings, future event dates, prices or legal eligibility claims.
editorial.sourcePolicy: Sources are recorded per thread with fetch date and claim coverage. Practical recommendations are editorial synthesis; protocol mechanics use primary documentation. See SOURCES.md for limitations and production notes.

threads.title: Build a portfolio someone can verify

posts.text: A Web3 portfolio needs a path from claim to evidence. For each project, show the problem, your contribution and something a reviewer can inspect. A title like 'growth lead' leaves all of that unanswered.

visual.headline: Make your work inspectable
visual.brief: Connect a project claim to a concrete artifact, with authorship marked between them.

posts.text: For an engineering sample, include a README with setup steps and tests for failure cases. Example: a withdrawal test should check what happens when the caller lacks permission, not only when the transfer succeeds.

visual.headline: Show the failure case
visual.brief: Compare two labeled test scenarios. This is a teaching diagram, not fabricated test output.

posts.text: For a marketing sample, write a campaign brief with an audience, a user action and a measurement plan. Example: a wallet tutorial can measure setup completion. Impressions alone won't tell you whether readers finished setup.

visual.headline: Connect content to an action
visual.brief: Map the proposed tutorial funnel without invented conversion rates.

posts.text: For community or operations work, show the system you built. A sample support runbook could explain how to collect an error report, assign an owner and tell the user when to expect an update.

visual.headline: Document a repeatable task
visual.brief: Draw a support ticket moving between user, moderator and engineer.

posts.text: Private work can still make a useful case study. Describe the constraint and your decision using approved, redacted material. Label a personal exercise as an exercise; don't turn it into a fictional client project.

visual.headline: Label the evidence honestly
visual.brief: Show three evidence formats with clear labels and no invented client identities.

posts.text: Before applying, open every portfolio link while logged out. Put the most relevant sample first, name your part in it and explain one limitation. A reviewer should be able to follow the evidence without requesting access.

visual.headline: Run the reviewer check
visual.brief: Use a compact pre-application checklist with one evidence link as the focal point.

supports.claims: Role-specific portfolios, runnable repositories, tests, documented nontechnical work, and accessible evidence links.
Authorship, confidentiality, accurate independent-work labels and logged-out link checks.

threads.title: Write resume bullets with evidence

posts.text: A resume bullet should give the interviewer something specific to ask about. 'Managed community' is a responsibility. 'Wrote a moderator handoff guide for unresolved support tickets' describes work they can discuss.

visual.headline: Give the interview a starting point
visual.brief: Contrast a vague role label with the components of a sample evidence-based bullet.

posts.text: Use this draft structure: action, scope, evidence. Example: 'Rewrote the wallet setup guide, added wrong-network screenshots and linked each step to product docs.' Use it only if it describes work you actually did.

visual.headline: Build one truthful bullet
visual.brief: Mark the example as sample wording. Highlight each component without repeating the full sentence.

posts.text: If you use a metric, include what you measured and when. Example format: 'Resolved [count] tickets during [period], excluding spam.' Keep the brackets until you have records. A made-up number weakens the whole application.

visual.headline: Give numbers a definition
visual.brief: Display blank metric fields with explicit placeholders, never realistic-looking invented results.

posts.text: Separate team outcomes from your contribution. If a product launch involved design, engineering and marketing, state the part you owned. A launch result doesn't prove that one person caused every change in usage.

visual.headline: Name your part in team work
visual.brief: Place a clearly bounded individual contribution inside the larger launch workflow.

posts.text: Match the order of your evidence to the role. Put support workflows first for operations, writing samples first for content, and tests first for engineering. Keep one full history, then select truthful details for each application.

visual.headline: Reorder without rewriting history
visual.brief: Show the same evidence library reordered for three different job tracks.

posts.text: Use the Resume Builder to organize projects, experience and skills, then check the exported PDF. Replace every sample entry, test its links and confirm the text copies cleanly. A template cannot verify your claims.

visual.headline: Check the exported resume
visual.brief: Capture the real Resume Builder project and experience controls. Crop out default names, salary claims and sample achievements.

supports.claims: Specific contributions, contextual metrics, attribution, tailored ordering, accurate labels and readable documents.
Existing project, experience and skills fields and PDF download control; default example entries must be replaced.

threads.title: Verify a job approach before opening files

posts.text: A convincing recruiter profile does not verify a job offer. Scammers can copy real people and company websites. Confirm the role and the person's identity through a company channel you find independently.

visual.headline: Verify through another channel
visual.brief: Show two separate contact routes meeting at a verification step. Avoid real recruiter identities.

posts.text: Open the company's careers page yourself and compare the role, application destination and contact details. A real job can still be used as bait by an impersonator, so a matching title is only the first check.

visual.headline: A matching title is insufficient
visual.brief: Use a comparison checklist rather than a fake job listing or a live vacancy screenshot.

posts.text: A take-home repository can contain malware. Don't run unfamiliar packages or scripts on a device holding work credentials or wallet keys. Ask for a written task and agree on an isolated test environment first.

visual.headline: Separate tests from valuable access
visual.brief: Draw an isolation boundary around an assessment environment without implying isolation guarantees safety.

posts.text: A request to install a custom meeting app or run a command to fix your camera deserves a pause. Use the meeting provider's official site and confirm the request with the hiring team through a separate channel.

visual.headline: Check the interview software
visual.brief: Show an unexpected software request diverted into a verification path, with no executable commands.

posts.text: Don't pay a deposit to receive a job or buy tokens to qualify for an interview. A recruiter also has no reason to ask for your seed phrase. Keep payroll details separate from early screening conversations.

visual.headline: Keep applications free of transfers
visual.brief: Mark the three requests as reasons to stop and verify. Do not display wallet addresses.

posts.text: Save the role URL, recruiter's contact and your independent confirmation in your application notes. Use job boards to find roles, then check the employer's application page. Neither a listing nor a polished profile is a guarantee.

visual.headline: Keep a verification record
visual.brief: Show a blank application-verification record, not current openings.

supports.claims: Recruiter impersonation, malicious take-home code, custom meeting software, independent contact verification and isolated assessment environments.
Fake job advertisements and requests for money or personal information; do not pay for the promise of a job.
Recovery phrases and private keys must not be shared.
Existing job discovery page only; no claim that any specific vacancy remains open.

threads.title: Questions to ask about a token-paid contract

posts.text: A token-paid contract needs more detail than a headline amount. Separate what you earn, when you earn it, when you can transfer it and how payment reaches you. Those can be different dates and different obligations.

visual.headline: Separate the compensation questions
visual.brief: Use parallel rows for earning, release and payment rather than a single pay-day marker.

posts.text: Ask whether the fee is a fixed number of tokens or a currency amount paid in tokens. For currency-denominated fees, specify the conversion source and time. Otherwise, both sides can calculate a different amount for the same invoice.

visual.headline: Define the unit of payment
visual.brief: Compare two contract payment models without prices, exchange rates or salary figures.

posts.text: Vesting describes when a grant is earned under its terms. A cliff delays initial vesting. Ask what happens if you leave before or after it, and whether separate transfer restrictions remain after tokens vest.

visual.headline: Read the vesting terms
visual.brief: Draw an undated illustrative timeline. Do not imply a standard grant length or guaranteed liquidity.

posts.text: Put the payer's legal name, scope, acceptance criteria and payment deadline in writing. For a content contract, specify whether the fee includes revisions, source files and translation. A token transfer won't settle a scope dispute.

visual.headline: Specify what the fee covers
visual.brief: Use a sample content contract outline with no invented parties or amounts.

posts.text: For an onchain payment, agree on the asset, network, recipient address and who covers fees. A token symbol alone is ambiguous. Confirm payment instructions through an agreed channel before anyone sends funds.

visual.headline: Write complete payment instructions
visual.brief: Display blank payment fields. Do not invent a usable recipient address.

posts.text: The Invoice Generator has payment, wallet and notes fields. Use the notes to record the agreed network and reference, then match the receipt to the invoice. Keep token grant terms in the contract rather than guessing them from a payment.

visual.headline: Match invoice to receipt
visual.brief: Capture real payment and notes controls. Crop default amounts, names, addresses and tax values.

supports.claims: Grant quantities, vesting and cliffs, volatility, and the need to clarify compensation terms. No salary amounts or universal vesting norms adopted.
Written deliverables, reviewers, payment token, chain and fee handling; payment records. These are contract questions, not legal conclusions.
Existing payment-method, wallet-address, notes and invoice fields.
Independent recipient and transaction checks before sending.

threads.title: Turn a DAO contribution into scoped work

posts.text: Before taking on DAO work, identify who can approve the task and who can authorize payment. A friendly reply in a chat may do neither. Start by reading the contributor process and a completed proposal with its payout record.

visual.headline: Find the approval path
visual.brief: Map distinct roles in a sample DAO workflow without assuming every DAO uses the same structure.

posts.text: Choose a small, inspectable first deliverable. Example: summarize one governance discussion with the proposal link, disputed points and open questions. Agree on scope before turning a helpful contribution into ongoing unpaid work.

visual.headline: Make the first task reviewable
visual.brief: Show the structure of a sample governance summary, with no invented proposal outcome.

posts.text: Write a task brief that names the output, format, reviewer and acceptance test. For a tutorial, 'a newcomer can complete the documented steps on the stated test network' is more useful than 'high-quality content'.

visual.headline: Define what completion means
visual.brief: Pair a tutorial deliverable with a concrete reader-completion check.

posts.text: Ask whether your payment needs a working-group approval, a vote or treasury signatures. Confirm the asset, network and expected payment step in the task thread. Different DAOs use different processes; a passed discussion is not a receipt.

visual.headline: Track approval and payment separately
visual.brief: Show a sample payment sequence with an explicit note that governance varies.

posts.text: Deliver a review packet: the work, a short change summary and the exact place to leave feedback. If the brief changes, record the new scope and payment agreement before continuing. Keep the acceptance decision with the task.

visual.headline: Make review easy to complete
visual.brief: Arrange a sample delivery packet around one review link.

posts.text: Keep a contribution log with scope, evidence, reviewer and payment status. Label volunteer work separately from paid work. It gives future collaborators a record they can check and helps you notice unfinished commitments.

visual.headline: Keep a contribution record
visual.brief: Use an empty contribution-log layout with field names, not fabricated client records.

supports.claims: Contributor research, scoped bounties, reviewer and payment terms, delivery packets and contribution logs. Governance timings, salary figures and blanket legal statements are excluded.
For DAOs using Safe, owners and signature thresholds control the standard transaction execution path.

threads.title: Write a job description you can assess

posts.text: A useful job description connects the work to the hiring process. For every requirement, decide what evidence would satisfy it. If 'Web3 native' has no clear assessment, replace it with the actual knowledge the role needs.

visual.headline: Connect requirements to evidence
visual.brief: Trace a requirement from an actual responsibility to a review method.

posts.text: Describe an output rather than a personality. Example: 'Maintain wallet onboarding docs and turn recurring support questions into updates' tells a content candidate more than 'obsessed with crypto and ready to hustle'.

visual.headline: Describe the output
visual.brief: Use an illustrative content-role brief centered on deliverables, not personality adjectives.

posts.text: Separate skills needed on arrival from skills you can teach. If the work requires clear technical writing, assess a writing sample. Familiarity with your team's publishing software may be something a new hire can learn.

visual.headline: Separate required from teachable
visual.brief: Compare day-one requirements with onboarding topics using the content-role example.

posts.text: State eligible work locations, overlap hours, on-call duties and the engagement type. 'Remote' leaves these questions open. If a role requires late-night incident coverage, describe the rota rather than implying constant availability.

visual.headline: Explain how the work happens
visual.brief: Show fields a recruiter should complete, without invented location permissions.

posts.text: Tell candidates what the assessment involves: task, time limit, review criteria and compensation. A sample support reply tests judgment. Asking for a complete launch campaign also asks for substantial usable work, so agree on payment and scope.

visual.headline: Scope the assessment upfront
visual.brief: Show an assessment brief with blank terms and two clearly labeled task examples.

posts.text: Draft the role in the JD Builder, then check each requirement against your interview plan. Remove default company details and sample pay. The final description should match what the manager can fund, review and support.

visual.headline: Review the role before publishing
visual.brief: Capture the real JD Builder controls. Crop all default employer, salary and vacancy details.

supports.claims: Outcome-led roles, required versus preferred skills, location clarity, and assessment scope. No hiring statistics, legal requirements or salary amounts adopted.
Existing responsibilities, qualifications, preferred qualifications and PDF controls; sample values are not employer facts.

threads.title: Prepare interview answers around decisions

posts.text: Prepare interview answers around decisions you made. Pick a real piece of work and explain the constraint, options, choice and result. That gives an interviewer more to assess than a list of tools you have used.

visual.headline: Explain a decision you made
visual.brief: Build a decision walkthrough with space for a real candidate's evidence.

posts.text: For an engineering answer, explain a failure you tested for and why it mattered. Example prompt: what should happen if a user rejects a wallet signature? Describe the interface state and how you would verify it.

visual.headline: Practice the rejected-signature case
visual.brief: Draw a proposed interface-state flow, labeled as an interview exercise rather than a product screenshot.

posts.text: For a community answer, explain how you handled uncertainty. A practice scenario: users report a failed withdrawal. Describe what you would verify, what you would say publicly and who should investigate before promising a fix.

visual.headline: Explain the response under uncertainty
visual.brief: Use the withdrawal-support scenario without implying that an incident actually occurred.

posts.text: For a marketing answer, define the user action behind the campaign. Explain the audience, channel choice and evidence you would collect. Be ready to separate attributed sign-ups from people who would have signed up anyway.

visual.headline: Explain what the campaign measures
visual.brief: Connect a proposed campaign to a measurement plan with no performance claims.

posts.text: If you lack a production example, say so and use a personal project or a clearly labeled scenario. Explain how you would check an unknown answer in the docs. Inventing an incident creates details you cannot defend in follow-up questions.

visual.headline: Separate experience from a proposal
visual.brief: Make the evidence status visible for each answer type.

posts.text: Use the Interview Question Bank to rehearse follow-up questions, not memorize paragraphs. After each answer, ask: what evidence supports it, what could fail and what trade-off did I choose? Recruiters can use the same checks consistently.

visual.headline: Practice the follow-up
visual.brief: Capture the actual question-bank navigation and scoring-guide area. Avoid implying it guarantees interview success.

supports.claims: Role-specific question sections, behavioral examples, follow-ups, trade-offs and scoring criteria. Sample scenarios are editorial exercises.
Defined metrics, individual attribution and truthful project descriptions.

threads.title: Write a technical content brief that teaches

posts.text: A technical content brief should name what the reader will be able to do afterward. 'Explain wallet approvals' is a topic. 'Help a user identify the spender and spending cap before approving' is a teachable task.

visual.headline: Give the reader a task
visual.brief: Contrast a broad topic with an actionable learning objective.

posts.text: Start with a real question from support, docs or user research. Example: 'Why does this transaction need another confirmation?' Record the source and context. Don't turn a question you invented into a claim about what customers ask.

visual.headline: Keep the question's context
visual.brief: Show a research note template with explicit evidence-status fields.

posts.text: Make a claim sheet before drafting: statement, primary source, network or version, and reviewer. If a feature exists on one chain, don't describe it as universal. Record which part of the source supports the statement.

visual.headline: Build a claim sheet
visual.brief: Show a blank four-column claim sheet rather than fake citations.

posts.text: Write the normal flow and one relevant failure case. For a wallet tutorial, include what the reader sees after rejecting a signature. Use a test account for screenshots and keep recovery phrases, customer details and private chats out of frame.

visual.headline: Teach the failure path too
visual.brief: Split a proposed tutorial into success and rejection branches, with no real wallet data.

posts.text: Ask a technical reviewer to check mechanics and a target reader to follow the steps. Give each a specific task: find an incorrect claim, or identify where you cannot continue. 'Any feedback?' leaves the review too open.

visual.headline: Give reviewers different jobs
visual.brief: Compare two review passes on the same tutorial.

posts.text: Publish with an owner and a revision trigger. A changed wallet screen or renamed function should prompt a check of the relevant steps. Keep the long guide as the reference, then use social posts to teach one specific part at a time.

visual.headline: Plan the next revision
visual.brief: Link a maintained guide to focused social excerpts and an explicit review loop.

supports.claims: Educational content, product tutorials, technical review, contributor guidance and distribution through focused social excerpts. Claim sheets and review prompts are editorial recommendations.
An approval screen identifies a spender and token spending cap.
Recovery phrases must not be exposed or included in screenshots.

threads.title: Build a useful community support queue

posts.text: A busy community chat can hide an unresolved support queue. Give each reported problem an owner and a status. 'We saw your message' is an acknowledgment; it does not tell the next moderator whether anyone is investigating.

visual.headline: Make unresolved work visible
visual.brief: Draw a proposed support queue with a named-owner field on each status, without fictional user tickets.

posts.text: Ask for the network, action attempted and exact error. Request a transaction hash only if relevant, and explain that it can reveal public wallet activity. Never ask for recovery phrases or private keys to investigate a support issue.

visual.headline: Collect only useful diagnostics
visual.brief: Use a support intake template with a visible warning against sending secrets.

posts.text: Route issues by what needs to happen. Example: a broken docs link goes to content; a reproducible transaction error goes to engineering; suspected phishing goes to the security contact. One moderator need not solve all three.

visual.headline: Route by the next action
visual.brief: Use three issue-to-owner paths. These are sample team roles, not a universal organization chart.

posts.text: During an incident, pin what is confirmed, what users should do and when the next update will appear. If the cause is unknown, say that. Keep a timestamped update log so moderators do not repeat different versions of the same answer.

visual.headline: Keep one incident update record
visual.brief: Show an empty status-update structure, not a simulated live incident announcement.

posts.text: Review repeated questions by topic, then fix the cause where possible. If users repeatedly miss a network selector, a clearer interface or guide may help more than another canned reply. Keep the original reports linked to the proposed change.

visual.headline: Turn repeated questions into fixes
visual.brief: Trace a hypothetical network-selection issue from support to a product improvement.

posts.text: At handoff, list unresolved issues, current owners and promised updates. Separate a first response from a resolution in your reporting. Otherwise, a fast acknowledgment can make a queue look healthier while users still wait for help.

visual.headline: Measure response and resolution separately
visual.brief: Use separate response and resolution milestones, with no invented service-level statistics.

supports.claims: Support, anti-phishing, transparent incident updates and feedback to engineering. Queue design and handoff fields are editorial synthesis; no constant-availability expectation adopted.
Support impersonation risk and the prohibition on sharing recovery phrases or private keys.
Public addresses and transactions can expose account activity in explorers.

threads.title: Write handoffs across time zones

posts.text: An async handoff should let someone continue while you are offline. Include the current state, evidence, next action and owner. A message that only says 'still working on it' leaves the next person with nothing to act on.

visual.headline: Leave enough to continue
visual.brief: Use a handoff card with an action field as the focal point.

posts.text: For engineering, link the exact branch or issue and explain what has already been tried. Example: 'Retry still fails after switching RPC provider; logs are in the issue.' This stops the next engineer from repeating the same investigation.

visual.headline: Record the attempted fix
visual.brief: Show a labeled hypothetical debugging handoff with no fabricated logs.

posts.text: For content, identify the approved draft, missing review and person who can sign it off. Example: 'Copy is ready; product needs to confirm the feature name.' A file named final-final does not explain why publishing is blocked.

visual.headline: State what blocks publication
visual.brief: Map a content handoff ending in a specific unresolved product question.

posts.text: Use a date and time zone for deadlines. 'By tomorrow' can mean different workdays. Agree whether response windows follow working hours, and give urgent incidents a separate escalation route rather than expecting everyone to monitor chat.

visual.headline: Make the deadline unambiguous
visual.brief: Compare an ambiguous deadline with a date-and-zone template; use placeholders, not an actual future appointment.

posts.text: Keep a decision record when a discussion changes the plan. Write the chosen option, reason, decider and what would trigger a review. Link it from the task so a teammate joining later can understand why the work took that direction.

visual.headline: Keep the reason with the decision
visual.brief: Attach a decision note to a work item, separate from the surrounding chat.

posts.text: Before logging off, read your handoff as if you had no chat history. Can you locate the work, understand the blocker and identify the next owner? Add the missing context now, while you still remember it.

visual.headline: Try the no-history check
visual.brief: Show a handoff checklist beside a muted chat-history panel, with no real messages.

supports.claims: Clear async updates, documented decisions, proactive communication and cross-time-zone context.
Named handoff owners, response expectations and decision logs. Only practical writing patterns are used, not the article's statistics, payroll or legal claims.

threads.title: Understand token approvals before signing

posts.text: An ERC-20 token approval gives another address permission to spend a specified token from your account. It is different from connecting a wallet to a website. Check the token, spender and amount before you approve.

visual.headline: Read the permission you are granting
visual.brief: Draw the relationship between token holder, token contract and approved spender. No real addresses.

posts.text: Example: you plan to swap 20 tokens, but the app requests an allowance of 200. That permission is larger than this trade. Where supported, set a cap that matches your intended use rather than accepting the requested amount automatically.

visual.headline: Compare the trade and the cap
visual.brief: Use two proportional bars labeled as a hypothetical token-quantity example, not prices.

posts.text: Disconnecting a website does not revoke an onchain token allowance. To remove that spending permission, submit a revocation on the relevant network and check that it confirms. An onchain revocation normally requires a network fee.

visual.headline: Disconnecting and revoking differ
visual.brief: Separate connection state from token-contract permission; show only revocation changing the allowance.

posts.text: A signature can authorize spending even when you pay no gas at signing. ERC-2612 permits let someone submit a signed approval onchain later. Read the spender, amount and deadline; a gasless prompt is not automatically a harmless login.

visual.headline: A signature can carry spending authority
visual.brief: Show signing followed by later onchain submission. Label the deadline as the permit submission deadline.

posts.text: NFT permissions use different scopes. setApprovalForAll can let an operator move every NFT you own from that collection contract. It is broader than approving one item, so check which collection and operator the request names.

visual.headline: Check the NFT permission scope
visual.brief: Compare single-item approval with all items under one collection contract, not all NFTs in a wallet.

posts.text: Review allowances by account and network, then remove ones you no longer need. Keep the approval and revocation receipts. Revoking permission cannot reverse a transfer that already happened, and it does not repair an exposed private key.

visual.headline: Keep an allowance review record
visual.brief: Show a permission inventory with no live balances. Distinguish permission cleanup from key compromise.

supports.claims: Token/spender/amount approval model, custom caps, collection-wide NFT operator approvals and limitations after assets are transferred.
Disconnecting differs from revocation, network-specific checks and onchain revocation gas fees.
Signed permits can be submitted by another address and include spender, value, nonce and deadline. The deadline limits permit submission, not the resulting allowance lifetime.
Private keys independently control accounts; permission revocation does not change a key.

threads.title: Separate seed phrases, keys and passwords

posts.text: In a seed-based wallet, the recovery phrase can restore the accounts derived from it. A private key controls an individual account. Treat either as access to funds, not as a support code you can share to fix a problem.

visual.headline: Know what each secret controls
visual.brief: Draw a phrase branching into account keys. Use abstract symbols, never sample recovery words.

posts.text: For MetaMask set up directly with a recovery phrase, the app password protects local access on that device. Changing it does not change the phrase. If someone copied the phrase, a new app password will not remove their access.

visual.headline: Local password and recovery differ
visual.brief: Scope the diagram to MetaMask's direct recovery-phrase setup, not social-login wallets.

posts.text: Keep a recovery-phrase backup offline and check the word order when recording it. A screenshot can sync to cloud storage. For a wallet using social login or another recovery design, read that wallet's actual recovery instructions.

visual.headline: Check your wallet's recovery method
visual.brief: Use a blank backup illustration with no words, QR codes or usable credentials.

posts.text: Two accounts derived from the same recovery phrase do not isolate a leaked phrase. Anyone with that phrase can derive both. Separating an experimental wallet from savings requires checking the keys and recovery setup, not just renaming accounts.

visual.headline: Account labels do not isolate keys
visual.brief: Show two account labels connected to one root secret. Avoid promising anonymity through wallet separation.

posts.text: A hardware wallet keeps signing keys on the device, but you can still approve a harmful transaction. Read the destination and permissions before confirming. Keeping the key offline and checking what you sign solve different problems.

visual.headline: Check the action as well as keys
visual.brief: Separate key storage from transaction review. Do not invent a branded hardware-wallet screen.

posts.text: Receiving a payment requires a public address on the agreed network, not a recovery phrase. If support, a recruiter or a website asks for your phrase, stop. Contact the service through its official help channel instead.

visual.headline: Share the receiving address only
visual.brief: Contrast public payment details with private recovery material without printing either.

supports.claims: Phrase-derived accounts, individual keys, setup-specific password roles, offline backups, word order and hardware wallets. Direct phrase setup is explicitly distinguished from social-login recovery.
Screenshot/cloud exposure, checking transactions and permissions, support impersonation and never sharing secrets.
Public account addresses are used to receive funds.

threads.title: Understand the route before bridging

posts.text: Changing the network in your wallet does not move your assets. Bridging uses a separate mechanism to transfer value or messages between chains. Start by naming the source chain, destination chain and exact asset you expect to receive.

visual.headline: A network switch is not a bridge
visual.brief: Separate a wallet's viewing selector from a cross-chain transfer route.

posts.text: A bridged token may represent an asset held on another chain. Its name can look familiar while its contract and redemption path differ. Check the destination asset in the issuer's or bridge's docs, rather than relying on the ticker.

visual.headline: Check what arrives on the other side
visual.brief: Use a generic wrapped-asset diagram without treating every bridge as lock-and-mint.

posts.text: Bridge risks depend on the design. Ask who verifies messages, who controls upgrades and whether anyone holds assets in custody. A bridge can depend on contracts, operators or both; the source chain's reputation does not answer these questions.

visual.headline: Identify the bridge's dependencies
visual.brief: Map separate trust dependencies instead of a single safe-or-unsafe score.

posts.text: Review the quoted output, fees and expected waiting steps before sending. Also check how you will pay for the next transaction on the destination chain. Receiving a token does not necessarily give you that chain's fee-paying asset.

visual.headline: Plan the destination transaction
visual.brief: Extend the bridge diagram through the user's next action. Include no live fees or completion-time promise.

posts.text: A confirmed source transaction is only one part of a cross-chain transfer. Check the bridge's status and the destination explorer before retrying. Save both transaction references when available so support can identify the correct transfer.

visual.headline: Track both sides of the transfer
visual.brief: Show distinct source and destination confirmations, with a pending middle stage.

posts.text: A small test transfer can help catch a wrong route or recipient, but it cannot prove a bridge is secure. Before a larger transfer, recheck the asset, address, fees and withdrawal path. Conditions can change between attempts.

visual.headline: A test checks the route
visual.brief: Distinguish route validation from bridge-security assessment without displaying transfer amounts.

supports.claims: Separate chains, wrapped assets, trusted/trust-minimized designs, custody, contract and operational risks. A successful transfer does not establish future security.
Network selection is distinct from bridging; review output and fees, submit, then wait for arrival. No fixed duration or unconditional return guarantee adopted.
Destination transactions on OP Mainnet require fee funding, an example of why a received token alone may not fund the next transaction.
Issuer support for native tokens does not automatically extend to third-party copies or wrappers. No jurisdiction-specific redemption advice used.

threads.title: Compare dollar-token mechanisms

posts.text: Two tokens can target the same dollar value while relying on different systems. Compare the backing, who can create or redeem tokens, and how the peg is maintained. A price target is not a guarantee of the price on every exchange.

visual.headline: Same target, different mechanisms
visual.brief: Use parallel mechanism columns without current prices or a safety ranking.

posts.text: Reserve-backed example: Circle describes USDC as backed by cash and cash-equivalent assets held separately from operating funds. Read reserve reports and applicable redemption terms. Holding a token and having direct issuer access are different things.

visual.headline: Read reserves and redemption terms
visual.brief: Connect issuer, reserves and token holder. Do not depict automatic redemption for every holder.

posts.text: Collateral-backed example: Aave users can borrow GHO against eligible supplied collateral. The borrowing position can be liquidated if it becomes undercollateralized under the protocol's rules. This mechanism differs from a bank-reserve-backed issuer.

visual.headline: Borrowing creates a collateral obligation
visual.brief: Scope the diagram to Aave's borrowing facilitator, not every possible GHO issuance path.

posts.text: Synthetic-dollar example: Ethena describes USDe as using backing assets and strategies including offsetting short futures positions. Read the trading and custody arrangements. This is a different mechanism from holding matching fiat reserves.

visual.headline: Identify the synthetic-dollar strategy
visual.brief: Illustrate a simplified hedged position. Do not present it as the full portfolio or as risk-free.

posts.text: Check how you would exit before choosing a payment asset. Selling on an exchange depends on its market and your access; redeeming with an issuer depends on its terms. A token trading near its target does not make those routes interchangeable.

visual.headline: Compare the exit routes
visual.brief: Draw two separate exit paths with conditions, no jurisdiction-specific eligibility claims.

posts.text: Keep holding, lending and reward products separate in your research. A yield offer adds a mechanism and its own conditions. Record the exact asset, backing, exit route and what generates any return before comparing headline yields.

visual.headline: Separate the token from the yield
visual.brief: Layer a lending or rewards product above an asset, showing added dependencies rather than a promised return.

supports.claims: Different stabilization mechanisms and separate lending uses. Promotional safety wording and yield ranges are excluded.
Circle's description of cash/cash-equivalent reserves, separation from operating funds and published reserve reporting.
No guaranteed secondary-market price, conditional redemption and no intrinsic holder yield. Specific redemption eligibility varies by applicable terms and is not asserted for all readers.
GHO borrowing against collateral via the Aave market facilitator and liquidation of borrowing positions.

USDe's synthetic-dollar design, backing and short-futures strategies, custody dependencies, distinct rewards product and conditional direct redemption. No fixed portfolio composition or return asserted.

threads.title: Read a transaction in a block explorer

posts.text: A transaction hash is a lookup reference, not proof that payment completed. Open it in an explorer for the correct network and check its status. A pending transaction has not yet been included in a block.

visual.headline: Look up the status, not just hash
visual.brief: Show a hash lookup leading to distinct pending, failed and successful states.

posts.text: Read the 'to' field carefully. In an Ethereum token transfer, it can name the token contract being called rather than the person receiving tokens. Check the decoded action and token-transfer details for the actual recipient and amount.

visual.headline: Contract destination and recipient can differ
visual.brief: Show sender calling a token contract, which updates the recipient's balance. No invented transaction hash.

posts.text: An Ethereum transaction can show zero ETH value while moving ERC-20 tokens. The value field records native ETH sent with the call. Token movements appear separately, so check the asset contract as well as the displayed symbol.

visual.headline: ETH value is not token value
visual.brief: Contrast the native-value field with a separate token-transfer record using abstract amounts.

posts.text: A failed Ethereum transaction can still consume gas because the network performed work before the failure. Read the failure reason if available. Don't interpret a fee deduction as proof that the intended transfer or contract action succeeded.

visual.headline: A fee can accompany failure
visual.brief: Separate the reverted action from the computation fee. Exclude transactions rejected before execution.

posts.text: A public explorer record shows addresses and actions, not necessarily the identities behind them. Match a payment to your agreed recipient, asset, network and reference. A screenshot of someone else's successful transfer is not your receipt.

visual.headline: Match the receipt to your payment
visual.brief: Compare agreed payment fields with explorer fields, avoiding personal wallet data.

posts.text: For a support report, keep the network, transaction hash, status and expected result together. Share the explorer link only with the context needed. It can reveal wallet activity, and support never needs your private key to read the public record.

visual.headline: Prepare a useful transaction report
visual.brief: Use a blank support-report template rather than a fabricated explorer screenshot.

supports.claims: Transaction status, hash, destination, token transfers, native value and public account history.
Transaction lifecycle, contract-call destination, native value and ERC-20 transfer calldata example.
Fees for executed failed transactions, contrasted with rejection before inclusion.
Network-specific explorers and public account activity lookup.
Never share private keys with support.

threads.title: Understand Ethereum and L2 transaction fees

posts.text: Gas measures computational work on Ethereum. The fee depends on both the gas used and the price per unit. A token transfer and a complex contract call can consume different amounts of work even when you send them at the same time.

visual.headline: Separate work from unit price
visual.brief: Show gas used multiplied by effective gas price, with no current fee estimates.

posts.text: For an ordinary Ethereum transaction, the effective price per gas includes the base fee and a priority fee. The base fee is burned; the priority fee goes to the validator. This describes Ethereum, not every chain's fee distribution.

visual.headline: Where Ethereum execution fees go
visual.brief: Split the execution fee into two destinations. Do not reuse this diagram as an OP Mainnet distribution chart.

posts.text: The transaction gas limit caps how much work can be used. Lowering it does not make the same operation need less work. If execution runs out of gas, the action reverts and the gas supplied for that execution is consumed.

visual.headline: A lower limit cannot reduce work
visual.brief: Compare sufficient and insufficient execution limits, distinct from pre-validation rejection.

posts.text: An L2 fee can include more than local execution. OP Mainnet documents execution, Ethereum data and operator fee components. Compare the total estimate for your action; one small gas-price number may leave out part of the cost.

visual.headline: Read the whole L2 fee
visual.brief: Use additive components with no values; make clear this is the documented OP Mainnet model, not every L2.

posts.text: An approval followed by a swap can require separate transactions and separate fees. Check which permissions you already have and what the app will submit. The fee for the swap alone may not describe the full workflow.

visual.headline: Count the actions in the workflow
visual.brief: Show a conditional approval step before the swap, allowing for other authorization designs.

posts.text: When comparing costs, use the same action, network and time of estimate. Record the fee-paying asset and any extra bridge or service charge. After execution, compare the receipt with the estimate to see which components actually applied.

visual.headline: Compare like-for-like fee estimates
visual.brief: Show a blank comparison worksheet. No cheapest-chain ranking or promised savings.

supports.claims: Gas as work, fee calculation, base-fee burn, priority fee, gas limits, out-of-gas execution and estimates.
OP Mainnet execution, L1 data and operator fee components; formula depends on active upgrades and chain parameters.
Approval is a separate onchain action in standard ERC-20 flows and has its own fee.
Bridge output and charges must be reviewed as part of a cross-chain workflow.

threads.title: Read an oracle feed beyond its price

posts.text: An Ethereum smart contract cannot fetch a website's data by itself during execution. An oracle brings external information onchain for contracts to use. That adds a data dependency you need to understand, even if the contract code is public.

visual.headline: Follow the external data path
visual.brief: Draw the data path, with a boundary between offchain collection and onchain consumption.

posts.text: Example: a lending contract uses a price feed to value collateral. If the feed is wrong or outdated, a correct calculation can still use a bad input. Check how the application handles unavailable or stale data.

visual.headline: Correct math can use bad data
visual.brief: Mark the price input as a dependency in a hypothetical lending calculation.

posts.text: A feed's units matter. Hypothetical example: an answer of 123400 with 4 decimals represents 12.34, not 123400. Read the feed's decimals and description rather than assuming every feed uses the same scale or currency pair.

visual.headline: Decode the feed's units
visual.brief: Show the fixed-point calculation as an invented teaching input, never a live market quote.

posts.text: Chainlink's latestRoundData returns an answer and updatedAt timestamp. The word 'latest' does not promise the value is recent enough for your application. Set a freshness rule appropriate to that feed and the action using it.

visual.headline: Check when the feed updated
visual.brief: Compare update time with a configurable freshness check; do not invent a universal timeout.

posts.text: Multiple oracle nodes are not the same as multiple independent data sources. If every node relies on the same upstream source, they can share its failure. Ask about source diversity as well as the number of reporters.

visual.headline: Count independent sources, not only nodes
visual.brief: Contrast several nodes using one source with nodes consulting independent sources.

posts.text: For an oracle-dependent feature, document the feed address, network, units, freshness rule and failure behavior. A product brief should explain what users can do when the feed is unavailable, rather than treating the data source as always working.

visual.headline: Document the oracle dependency
visual.brief: Use a feature-review checklist usable by both engineering and content teams.

supports.claims: Deterministic execution, external data delivery, collateral pricing, correctness/availability risks and distinction between node and data-source diversity.
decimals, description, latestRoundData, answer and updatedAt; network-specific feed configuration. Numeric example is arithmetic, not reported market data.

threads.title: Understand upgradeable contract control

posts.text: A contract address can stay the same while the logic users reach changes. An upgradeable proxy forwards calls to an implementation contract. Updating that implementation reference changes behavior without giving users a new proxy address.

visual.headline: Same address, different implementation
visual.brief: Show the proxy's target changing while the user's entry address stays fixed.

posts.text: In a delegatecall-based proxy, the implementation supplies code while the proxy holds the state. That separation lets a new implementation work with existing balances or settings. It also makes storage compatibility an important upgrade concern.

visual.headline: Separate code from stored state
visual.brief: Keep state attached to the proxy as the implementation changes. Scope to delegatecall-based proxies.

posts.text: Ask who can authorize an upgrade. It might be one address, a multisig or a governance process. Read the actual authorization path; a project calling itself decentralized does not tell you which party can change its contract behavior.

visual.headline: Find the upgrade authority
visual.brief: Show alternative authority models without assigning an unsupported safety score.

posts.text: Source verification checks a relationship between published code and deployed bytecode. It is not an audit or a promise that the logic is safe. For a proxy, inspect the implementation and its controls as well as the proxy's own verified code.

visual.headline: Verification is one check
visual.brief: Separate source matching from security analysis. Do not draw a verified badge as a safety guarantee.

posts.text: Example review: a protocol says a parameter change has a delay. Check whether the upgrade authority can replace the logic without that same delay. Reviewing one restricted function is incomplete if another permission can bypass its restriction.

visual.headline: Check the alternate control path
visual.brief: Label this as a hypothetical review question, not a discovered vulnerability in a named protocol.

posts.text: Keep a contract review note with the network, proxy, implementation and upgrade authority. Record when you checked them. An old audit or saved source page may describe an earlier implementation rather than the code users reach today.

visual.headline: Record which implementation you reviewed
visual.brief: Use an implementation review record with no invented addresses, audits or dates of deployment.

supports.claims: Proxy forwarding, replaceable implementations, proxy state, storage compatibility and upgrade governance. The delay-bypass scenario is a hypothetical implication of upgrade control.
Source verification compares compilation outputs with deployed code and is distinct from correctness/security verification. No tool-specific universal match guarantee asserted.

threads.title: Understand multisig approvals and execution

posts.text: A multisig threshold specifies how many owners must authorize an action. In a 2-of-3 Safe, the standard owner-signature path requires two owners. That reduces dependence on one key, but the threshold alone does not describe every permission.

visual.headline: Read the threshold and the permissions
visual.brief: Show three distinct owners with two authorizations, clearly scoped to the standard owner-signature path.

posts.text: Two signing keys held by one person do not provide two independent reviewers. Agree who checks the recipient, asset and purpose before signing. A threshold can enforce a signature count; it cannot tell whether anyone read the payment request.

visual.headline: Separate signatures from independent review
visual.brief: Contrast multiple keys under one operator with genuinely independent review.

posts.text: Collecting enough signatures does not itself mean the transfer happened. A Safe transaction still needs onchain execution. For treasury reporting, distinguish proposed, signed, executed and confirmed payments instead of treating approval as receipt.

visual.headline: Approval is not a payment receipt
visual.brief: Use a payment lifecycle with execution clearly separated from offchain signature collection.

posts.text: Safe modules can execute through a separate path that bypasses the usual owner-signature checks. Review enabled modules and what each can do. A screenshot showing a multisig threshold leaves out this part of the account's authority.

visual.headline: Review the module path
visual.brief: Draw module execution separately from threshold approval. Do not imply every Safe has a module enabled.

posts.text: Plan for unavailable signers before a payment is urgent. In the 2-of-3 example, one missing owner still leaves two; two missing owners block the standard path. Write down owner replacement and recovery procedures while access is available.

visual.headline: Test signer availability
visual.brief: Show availability cases for the standard threshold path, with modules and recovery treated separately.

posts.text: For each treasury payment, keep the request, reviewer checks and execution receipt together. Review owners, threshold and modules when responsibilities change. The account configuration and the team's payment process both need to match current authority.

visual.headline: Keep the payment record complete
visual.brief: Connect an operational payment record to an account-permission review, with no real treasury details.

supports.claims: Owners, thresholds, signature validation, execTransaction, module execution bypass and owner/threshold changes. Independent-review and recordkeeping steps are editorial operational recommendations.

threads.title: Understand Solana mint and token accounts

posts.text: On Solana, a mint account identifies a token, while a token account records holdings for an owner. These are different addresses with different jobs. Knowing the distinction helps when an explorer shows more accounts than your wallet interface does.

visual.headline: Mint and token accounts differ
visual.brief: Map a mint to separate holders' token accounts and their owner addresses.

posts.text: A Solana mint stores information such as supply, decimals and optional mint or freeze authorities. The mint authority can create more units; the freeze authority can freeze token accounts. Check the actual fields instead of inferring powers from a name.

visual.headline: Read the token's authority fields
visual.brief: Show optional authority fields without implying that all mints retain them.

posts.text: A token account holds units of one mint for one owner. A wallet can own multiple token accounts, even for the same mint. For a balance investigation, check the owner and mint rather than assuming the first account is the complete picture.

visual.headline: One wallet can own several accounts
visual.brief: Draw one owner connected to two token accounts for the same mint.

posts.text: An associated token account, or ATA, is the standard derived token account for an owner and mint under a token program. Creating it requires an account-storage balance. The payer can fund that account even when another wallet owns it.

visual.headline: Account payer and owner can differ
visual.brief: Show a payer funding creation while ownership belongs to the recipient. Include no current storage cost.

posts.text: A Solana transaction can contain several instructions, such as creating a token account and transferring tokens. If an instruction fails during execution, the transaction's changes revert together. Execution fees can still be charged on failure.

visual.headline: Instructions succeed or revert together
visual.brief: Group two hypothetical instructions inside one atomic transaction boundary.

posts.text: When checking a Solana token receipt, identify the network, transaction status, mint, destination token account and its owner. A familiar symbol alone does not establish that you received the intended asset in the intended wallet.

visual.headline: Follow the token receipt to its owner
visual.brief: Use a generic explorer-reading checklist rather than invented account records or balances.

supports.claims: Mint identity and authority fields, one-mint token accounts, multiple accounts per owner, associated token accounts and account-storage payer.
Transactions contain instructions, execute atomically, and can incur fees on execution failure. No changing packet, timing or fee constants used.

threads.title: Compare cities against a real workweek

posts.text: Compare cities against your workweek before comparing their overall scores. A recruiter taking private calls and an engineer working mostly asynchronously need different setups. Write down the conditions your work actually requires.

visual.headline: Start with the workweek
visual.brief: Compare two hypothetical work patterns without assigning them to nationalities or income levels.

posts.text: Make two lists: requirements and preferences. Example requirements might be a private call space and workable team overlap. Walkability or warm weather may be preferences. A high overall score should not hide a missing requirement.

visual.headline: Separate requirements from preferences
visual.brief: Show a sample decision matrix with unscored fields, not invented city ratings.

posts.text: Use the city directory to compare living-cost estimates, internet, safety, walkability and weather. Change the ranking category to match your question. Sorting by internet answers a different question from sorting by living costs.

visual.headline: Change the comparison question
visual.brief: Capture the real nomads ranking selector and Compare controls. Crop live costs, rankings and counts.

posts.text: Treat city-level information as a starting point for checking the actual place. Ask a host about the desk, call privacy and internet at the accommodation. A city's average cannot tell you whether a particular room suits your work.

visual.headline: Check the actual room
visual.brief: Zoom conceptually from city to neighborhood to room, without invented property photographs.

posts.text: Compare the months you would be there, not only an annual weather summary. Also map team meetings to your local hours for those dates. A city can fit your preferences while the working schedule still does not fit your day.

visual.headline: Use the dates you would stay
visual.brief: Connect an undated sample stay calendar to weather and schedule checks. Avoid forecasts and country claims.

posts.text: End with a shortlist and an unanswered-questions column. For each city, note what needs a host quote, an employer answer or an official entry check. A useful comparison shows what you still need to verify before booking.

visual.headline: Keep the unknowns beside the shortlist
visual.brief: Use a blank shortlist worksheet so the reader supplies cities and personal requirements.

supports.claims: City comparison/ranking categories and estimated-cost context. Work-pattern and shortlist methods are editorial recommendations.
Workspace choice depends on noise, calls, amenities, commute and personal work requirements.
Workspace, connection and correct calendar time-zone checks.

threads.title: Turn cost estimates into a personal worksheet

posts.text: A city's estimated monthly cost is not a quote for your stay. Use it to shortlist places, then replace assumptions with accommodation and workspace quotes for your dates. Keep the estimate and the quoted amount in separate columns.

visual.headline: Separate estimates from quotes
visual.brief: Show an empty estimate-versus-quote worksheet; no city price or personal budget assumption.

posts.text: Group costs by how they occur: recurring, one-off and refundable deposits. A deposit may come back later, but you still need the cash upfront. Keeping it separate avoids confusing total spending with cash tied up during the stay.

visual.headline: Separate spending from tied-up cash
visual.brief: Show cash-flow categories with blank amounts, and a conditional return arrow for deposits.

posts.text: Compare accommodation and workspace together. A room without a usable desk may require coworking plus transport. A higher room quote could include what you need. Check the combined setup rather than choosing on rent alone.

visual.headline: Compare the complete working setup
visual.brief: Compare two hypothetical accommodation setups with line items but no monetary values.

posts.text: Ask what the quote excludes: utilities, cleaning, workspace access or payment fees. Record the currency and the conversion date if you compare currencies. A copied price without its inclusions can make two options look more similar than they are.

visual.headline: Keep the quote's conditions
visual.brief: Annotate a generic quote-field diagram. Do not invent a property quote or exchange rate.

posts.text: Build an expected case and a disruption case using your own quotes. Example: a canceled booking could add temporary lodging and another transfer. Name the extra items rather than inserting a universal emergency-budget percentage.

visual.headline: Model a specific disruption
visual.brief: Label the canceled-booking case hypothetical; leave all amounts for the reader.

posts.text: Before committing, check the total due now, recurring costs, refund conditions and what remains uncertain. Keep links to the quotes beside each line item. That makes the plan easy to update when your dates or working needs change.

visual.headline: Keep the worksheet updateable
visual.brief: Finish with a source-linked planning worksheet, without implying the site calculates personal runway.

supports.claims: Cost estimates as comparison inputs. The personal worksheet, deposit separation and disruption case are editorial planning methods, not site features or promised costs.
Workspace fees, amenities and commute costs should be considered alongside accommodation.

threads.title: Research permission for the work you plan

posts.text: Permission to enter, stay and work are separate questions. Visa-free entry does not automatically authorize remote work. Research the activity you plan to do and the length of stay, rather than treating an entry label as a complete answer.

visual.headline: Separate entry, stay and work
visual.brief: Use separate permission questions, with no country-specific eligibility conclusions.

posts.text: Write a short description of your situation before researching: passport, residence, work type, employer or clients, and intended stay. A salaried employee and a freelancer may need different evidence. Don't assume one person's approval applies to you.

visual.headline: Define the case you are researching
visual.brief: Show a private research profile with blank fields and no nationality-specific example.

posts.text: The visa directory lets you research program requirements and stay references, with links to official sources. Use its income figures as a screening reference, then check the authority's current amount, currency and evidence rules.

visual.headline: Follow the program to its source
visual.brief: Capture real Visa programs controls and the official-source link. Crop country amounts and stay durations.

posts.text: Ask how income must be documented. Are invoices, employment letters or account statements required? If you receive tokens, ask whether and how that income is accepted as evidence. A wallet balance alone does not answer the program's requirements.

visual.headline: Check acceptable income evidence
visual.brief: Present document questions, not a universal required-document list or acceptance guarantee.

posts.text: Check dependent rules, insurance, application location and renewal conditions before planning around a program. Keep employer permission in a separate column. An employer's approval to travel does not establish immigration permission, or the reverse.

visual.headline: Keep different approvals separate
visual.brief: Show official program checks beside employer checks without conflating them.

posts.text: Save the official source URL, date checked and the exact question you still need answered. If a requirement is unclear, ask the issuing authority or a qualified adviser about your circumstances before making nonrefundable plans.

visual.headline: Keep a dated research record
visual.brief: Use a blank source log and question field, without reproducing legal thresholds.

supports.claims: Separate program and passport-checker modes, requirements, approximate income references, stay references and official links. This is a research workflow, not advice on any country's rules.
Entry-document research includes passport, visa and health requirements and needs current sources. This page is not cited as work-authorization advice.

threads.title: Use a passport checker without losing conditions

posts.text: Two colleagues planning the same trip can face different entry conditions because they hold different passports. Use the passport you will actually travel on, then check the destination, purpose and dates. Another person's experience is not your eligibility.

visual.headline: Check the traveler, not just destination
visual.brief: Show two blank traveler profiles for one destination without national flags or assumed outcomes.

posts.text: Entry labels leave details to verify. Check whether you must apply before departure, complete a process on arrival or meet conditions for an exemption. 'Visa required' alone does not tell you whether an online application is available.

visual.headline: Read beyond the entry label
visual.brief: Turn broad entry categories into research questions, without country-specific answers.

posts.text: Our passport checker separates checked baselines, historical evidence and unresolved reviews. Read the conditions and source date behind a result. A historical reference can help research a rule, but it is not proof that the rule still applies.

visual.headline: Read the evidence status
visual.brief: Capture genuine checker evidence labels and Conditions & sources controls. Crop destination-specific entry outcomes.

posts.text: Use the checker for its stated passport and visitor scope. Check whether your residence, other visas, passport type or purpose changes the conditions. A tourist-entry baseline is not a work permit or a promise of admission.

visual.headline: Check whether the baseline fits you
visual.brief: Keep scope visible above a personal-conditions checklist; show no guaranteed result.

posts.text: Review the whole route, including transit stops. Ask the airline what documents it will check, and verify immigration conditions with official sources. Passport validity, onward travel or prior approval may need checking even when a visa is not required.

visual.headline: Check the whole travel route
visual.brief: Draw a generic route with a document-check point at each stage, without naming countries.

posts.text: Keep a dated entry checklist with links to the official conditions and any written clarification. Recheck it before departure. Use the map to organize research; use the underlying conditions to decide what documents and permissions you need.

visual.headline: Turn the map into a checklist
visual.brief: Move from a generic map view to a source-linked document checklist, not a passport ranking.

supports.claims: Passport-specific visitor references, application-method caveat, conditions, source dates, and checked/historical/unresolved distinctions. Implementation inspected to confirm dynamically rendered capabilities.
Current passport, visa and health documentation research for air travel. Checklist items are questions to verify, not universal entry requirements.

threads.title: Choose a popup community by its working format

posts.text: A popup village, permanent coliving space and city project are different kinds of commitment. Start by checking the format and who operates it. A community directory listing does not establish current availability or what is included in a stay.

visual.headline: Choose the format first
visual.brief: Capture the real Popups type filters. Crop dates, prices, membership counts and availability claims.

posts.text: Name the reason you would join. Example: get feedback on a prototype, write alongside other researchers or meet people working on governance. Then look for a format that supports that activity, rather than choosing only from photos.

visual.headline: Match the community to your purpose
visual.brief: Match illustrative work goals to session types without promising a particular community delivers them.

posts.text: Ask what a normal workday looks like: quiet hours, calls, workshops and optional social time. Someone with client meetings may need different space from a person coding all afternoon. Get details about the actual venue before committing.

visual.headline: Ask about the ordinary workday
visual.brief: Use an illustrative day layout with no announced event dates or venue promises.

posts.text: Check what participation covers: accommodation, workspace, meals, sessions and any application process. Ask about cancellation and accessibility needs directly. The word 'community' does not specify what a booking includes.

visual.headline: Confirm the participation terms
visual.brief: Show questions for an organizer, not a made-up package or offer.

posts.text: Offer a contribution you can realistically deliver. Example: a documentation review hour or a session on handling support reports. Tell the organizer who it is for, what attendees should bring and what they can leave with.

visual.headline: Offer a specific contribution
visual.brief: Use a sample documentation-review session brief with no real event branding.

posts.text: Before booking, confirm current details with the organizer and check your own entry and work permissions. Keep the community fit, travel eligibility and employment arrangements as separate decisions. A good fit in one area does not settle the others.

visual.headline: Keep the booking checks distinct
visual.brief: Use separate checks converging on a personal decision, without implying approval or availability.

supports.claims: Directory spans popup, permanent and city/SEZ formats. Selection and organizer questions are editorial guidance, not claims about specific communities or future events.
Workspace noise, amenities and work-style trade-offs.
Specific contributions, peer feedback and clear deliverables in communities.
Entry/program research is separate from community participation. No legal outcome implied.

threads.title: Host a coworking session with a useful output

posts.text: Give a coworking session a small, visible output. Example: each person leaves with a reviewed README or a clearer onboarding page. A defined task helps newcomers decide whether the session fits them and what to bring.

visual.headline: Define what people can finish
visual.brief: Label two possible session outputs as examples, not completed community projects.

posts.text: Write the invitation around the work: who it suits, required preparation, language, venue or call link, and time zone. State whether beginners can observe. Avoid making people guess whether they need code, a wallet or prior protocol knowledge.

visual.headline: Make the invitation specific
visual.brief: Use an undated invitation template, with no invented event or sign-up destination.

posts.text: Try an example 80-minute format: 10 minutes to name tasks, 50 minutes of quiet work and 20 minutes for optional feedback. Publish the format in advance so someone who needs focused work can decide whether it suits them.

visual.headline: An example coworking format
visual.brief: Draw a proportional 80-minute teaching agenda, clearly labeled as a suggested format rather than an upcoming event.

posts.text: Use a shared task board with a specific request beside each item. 'Check whether this setup guide skips a step' is easier to answer than 'feedback welcome'. Let people choose whether to share publicly or work privately.

visual.headline: Ask for a specific review
visual.brief: Show an empty task board with one labeled sample review question, not a fake software screenshot.

posts.text: Ask before recording, taking photos or publishing someone's work. For a wallet-related session, use demonstration accounts without valuable funds and keep secrets off shared screens. Participants should know what will be visible before they join.

visual.headline: Agree on what will be shared
visual.brief: Use a host checklist. Never include a sample seed phrase or actual participant image.

posts.text: After the session, share agreed notes and unfinished questions with an owner for each follow-up. Ask which part helped people do their work. Use that feedback to decide whether to repeat the format, change the task or keep the group smaller.

visual.headline: Close the session with follow-through
visual.brief: Connect session outputs to a simple follow-up record, with no attendance or outcome claims.

supports.claims: Peer reviews, scoped contributions, cross-time-zone communication, appropriate public/private channels and follow-through. The agenda and consent checklist are editorial recommendations, not researched optimal durations.
Educational workshops, welcoming newcomers and collecting feedback as community work.
Protect recovery phrases and private keys from exposure, including screenshots.

threads.title: Test a remote workspace before relying on it

posts.text: A room with Wi-Fi is not yet a tested workspace. Check it with the tasks you actually do: a video call, a file upload or access to your work systems. A speed-test screenshot alone cannot show whether the setup suits your working day.

visual.headline: Test your actual work
visual.brief: Show task-based checks rather than a claimed minimum internet speed.

posts.text: Ask for a photo of the actual desk and chair, and check where calls can happen privately. A dining table in a shared room may work for writing but fail during a confidential interview. Match the space to the task.

visual.headline: Check the desk and call space
visual.brief: Compare writing and confidential-call needs with diagrams, not invented accommodation photos.

posts.text: Test the backup connection rather than merely owning one. Can your laptop connect to the hotspot and reach the tools you need? Check local coverage and account conditions with the provider; a second connection is useful only if it works where you are.

visual.headline: Test the backup connection
visual.brief: Show an actual-work connectivity test without endorsing a provider or promising coverage.

posts.text: Check power access, charging cables and where you would work during an outage. If your role has a response commitment, agree on a fallback with the team. The plan might be another workspace or a named colleague covering the urgent task.

visual.headline: Plan around a power interruption
visual.brief: Map a hypothetical interruption to practical fallback options, with no local reliability claims.

posts.text: Before travel, check backups and account recovery while your normal setup is available. Keep recovery codes protected and follow your employer's device policy. Losing a phone should not be the first time you discover how work-account recovery works.

visual.headline: Check access recovery before departure
visual.brief: Use general work-account recovery fields; distinguish account codes from wallet seed phrases.

posts.text: Use the Remote Work Checklist as a starting point, then adapt it to your role. Add a real call test, backup-connection test and recovery check. The useful result is a setup you have checked, not every box ticked on someone else's equipment list.

visual.headline: Adapt the checklist to your work
visual.brief: Capture genuine checklist section headings and controls. Crop hardware-size recommendations and unrelated defaults.

supports.claims: Workspace, camera/microphone, communication tools, backups, security and power-readiness topics. Tests and adaptation are editorial advice, not a universal hardware specification.
Reliable connectivity, mobile backup, workspace separation and communication requirements.
Workspace privacy, amenities and alternatives depend on the work.

threads.title: Check whether a remote role fits your location

posts.text: A remote job can still limit where you may work. Before applying or planning travel, check eligible locations, employment arrangements and required overlap. 'Remote' describes part of the setup, not permission to work from any country.

visual.headline: Read the remote conditions
visual.brief: Use location-condition fields, not current job listings or country-specific eligibility examples.

posts.text: Ask two separate questions: 'Can you hire someone living where I live?' and 'Can I temporarily work elsewhere?' The answers may differ. Get the relevant policy in writing rather than treating a remote label as approval for a trip.

visual.headline: Hiring location and travel can differ
visual.brief: Compare permanent hiring eligibility with temporary work-from-elsewhere permission.

posts.text: Translate required overlap into your local hours for the dates involved. Ask whether the team means fixed UTC hours or local business hours that change seasonally. 'Some overlap' is too vague to plan regular calls or on-call coverage.

visual.headline: Translate overlap into actual hours
visual.brief: Show two blank schedule rows with an overlap band. Do not assert fixed country offsets.

posts.text: Clarify which entity signs the agreement and whether the role is employment or contracting. Ask who handles payroll, benefits and required paperwork. Receiving money in crypto does not answer those questions or establish permission to work abroad.

visual.headline: Identify the working arrangement
visual.brief: Keep payment technology separate from the legal and employment questions; no classification advice.

posts.text: Check whether travel affects access to customer data, internal systems or signing duties. An operator responsible for treasury approvals may need a different travel plan from a writer with read-only access. Ask the owner of each relevant policy.

visual.headline: Check the access your role needs
visual.brief: Map task responsibilities to policy questions without asserting universal location restrictions.

posts.text: Keep an eligibility note beside each application: allowed location, overlap, agreement type and unanswered questions. Confirm changes before moving. That gives you and the recruiter a shared reference instead of relying on different meanings of 'remote'.

visual.headline: Keep the eligibility answer with the role
visual.brief: Show a blank application note, with no live vacancy, employer promise or compensation amount.

supports.claims: Existing job-discovery page; no claim about a specific opening or its continued availability.
Location, time-zone overlap, work model, working conditions and engagement details should be explicit. Personal eligibility and classification are not inferred.
Calendar time zones, access to work systems and security preparation.
Immigration and work-permission research remains separate from payment method.

threads.title: Read citizenship references beyond the minimum

posts.text: Treat a citizenship directory entry as a research reference. Check the route's status and whether the authority currently accepts applications. An announced route or unverified intake is not the same as an open program you can apply to.

visual.headline: Check status before comparing routes
